transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Priya Chen (Redwood Solutions), Jordan (CTO - Catalyst), Priya N. (Head of Platform), Samir (SecOps), Alex (ML Engineer), Lina (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be incomplete): Discussed POC boundaries, success metrics, sketches for SDK integration and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Agreed to share security docs and benchmark artifacts.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round of intros and then we'll jump into the POC goals.
[00:22] Jordan (Catalyst): Hi, Jordan here, CTO. We're looking to accelerate claims automation, reduce manual triage and speed up response times.
[00:35] Priya N.: Priya, head of platform — mostly concerned about latency, cost, and how this will plug into our existing event pipeline.
[00:47] Samir: Samir, security ops, will be validating compliance and key management.
[01:02] Maya: Great. Ethan from our infra team will walk through the technical approach. Ethan?
[01:12] Ethan (Redwood): Thanks. High level, Redwood can offer three modes for the POC: hosted API for quick iteration, Redwood Dedicate — sorry, Dedicated reserved capacity — for predictable throughput, or Private (VPC) if you need network isolation. For integration we support our SDKs and also OpenAI-compatible endpoints so you can swap calls with minimal code changes.
[01:36] Alex (Catalyst): When you say OpenAI-compatible, will function/tool calling work the same way? We have an existing tool orchestration layer.
[01:48] Ethan: Yes, function calling is supported. There are a few caveats around streaming + tool invocation ordering, but our SDK exposes the same primitives. There may be slight differences in metadata fields — we've seen some transcribe issues in older docs where the key was called 'function_name' vs 'toolId'. We'll provide a compat shim.
[02:15] Lina: Our product wants structured JSON output to feed into rule engines. How rigorously can you enforce a schema?
[02:25] Ethan: We recommend a JSON schema enforcement layer on your side, but Redwood offers structured output hints and model prompts. For POC we can add post-processing validators in the pipeline and measure schema compliance as a metric.
[02:42] Priya Chen (Redwood Solutions): For success criteria, we typically break into latency (P95), throughput, and correctness. Jordan, what do you think is acceptable for latency?
[02:53] Jordan: Ideally P95 under 300ms, but if that's too aggressive at scale we could accept sub-350ms for our initial 1k qps baseline. Cost is also a factor — we're comparing against Anthropic and Bedrock.
[03:12] Ethan: 350ms P95 is doable on Dedicated with tuned batch profiles for short completions. We'll need realistic prompt lengths to plan. What is your typical token count?
[03:25] Alex: For claims summaries our average is about 80 tokens per request, sometimes up to 300 when we include full notes.
[03:36] Ethan: Got it. For planning, we'll size baseline at 1k qps with a 3x burst to 3k for spikes. That suggests we'd recommend a 2-3 GPU Dedicated pool depending on model and quantization. We'll include quantized variants in the benchmarks.
[03:58] Samir: For security, we need SOC2 reports, encrypted logs, KMS integration, and audit trails that include per-request metadata. Also we require data residency in eu-west-1 for regulatory reasons. Can Redwood support that?
[04:16] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private can be deployed into your VPC or we can host regionally for eu-west-1. We integrate with customer KMS providers and provide audit logs; we'll send the SOC-2 and ISO artifacts in the security pack.
[04:29] Samir: Great, please include details on log retention and redaction controls.
[04:36] Maya: Will do.
[04:40] [05:00] Speaker 1: There's a question around model parity — if we run the hosted model for dev and Dedicated for prod, will outputs match?
[05:12] Ethan: Short answer: there can be small nondeterministic diffs, especially across quantized kernels and different hardware families. For POC we'll pin model versions and provide regression tests using your prompt set to measure drift. We also offer continuous evals to catch regressions.
[05:36] Priya N.: What's the typical turnaround for a benchmark run? We want several runs across the week.
[05:46] Ethan: For the initial pass using our benchmark harness, end-to-end including ingestion and metric computation, roughly 4-6 hours for a couple hundred thousand requests depending on queuing. We'll give you a template to run locally or use our hosted harness.
[06:02] Jordan: We also integrate outputs into our existing event bus — will streaming responses complicate things?
[06:12] Ethan: Streaming is supported but you have to deal with partial outputs; for schema enforcement we usually recommend final response validation. If you need function/tool calling in the middle of a stream, we can orchestrate with callbacks. There's a small chance of reordering in very heavy load; we'll capture traces.
[06:36] Lina: On the SDK side — do you have a Java SDK? Our platform is Java heavy.
[06:44] Maya: Yes we have official SDKs for Node and Python and a maintained Java SDK from the community which we can support; for POC we'll provide sample clients and integration snippets.
[06:58] Alex: The sample client needs to include automatic retry, idempotency keys, and token usage logging.
[07:08] Ethan: Those are standard in our SDK. We'll include examples for idempotency keys and per-request tracing headers so you can join traces with your APM.
[07:28] Priya Chen: Let's talk metrics for correctness. Alex, can you define the evaluation metric?
[07:34] Alex: For entity extraction and field filling we want F1 > .92 on the benchmark set, and for summary fidelity a ROUGE-L threshold — but main thing is downstream automations should have >85% pass rate without manual intervention.
[07:50] Ethan: We'll measure exact match for required fields and schema compliance as separate metrics. We'll include confusion matrices and per-field F1.
[08:05] [08:20] Speaker 2: There's mention of KV cache — how does it behave across sharded replicas?
[08:30] Ethan: Our runtime maintains local KV caches per replica for latency, and we support warm cache seeding for common prefixes. For multi-replica consistency we use a policy-based staleness model; for the POC we'll document behaviors and recommend warmup strategies. Sometimes docs show 'KV cash' in the transcript — sorry for the typo.
[08:56] Samir: For auditability we need per-token cost breakdown and who invoked what.
[09:06] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns tied to API keys and routes. We'll demo the console in the next session.
[09:18] Jordan: What about fallback strategies? If Dedicated pool is saturated do you route to hosted variants?
[09:26] Ethan: Yes, smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants or other regions. You can configure policy to prioritize latency or cost. We'll show policy examples in the playbook.
[09:40] Priya N.: For the POC we need a clearly defined runbook with acceptance criteria and rollbacks.
[09:48] Maya: We'll provide a POC playbook with success criteria, runbook, and a rollback plan.
[09:54] 
[10:10] Alex: A few implementation nitpicks — how do you handle structured output when model hallucinates fields?
[10:20] Ethan: We combine prompt engineering with deterministic decoding (e.g., top-p constraints, temperature down) and post-hoc validators. For critical fields we use forced tokens or enumerated values to reduce hallucination. We'll surface hallucination rate in the benchmark.
[10:41] Lina: Timeline — what is realistic for a 4-week pilot?
[10:47] Maya: Proposed timeline: Week 0: sign-off + security review; Week 1: integration and sample data ingestion; Week 2: benchmark runs + iterate; Week 3: evaluation and SLO tuning; Week 4: findings + proposal for next phase. So about 4 weeks with a couple of blockers depending on security review.
[11:08] Jordan: That works if we can get the security pack quickly.
[11:12] Maya: We'll prioritize that.
[11:16] 
[11:35] Priya N.: Cost modeling — can you provide cost estimates per 1M tokens for dedicated vs hosted?
[11:44] Ethan: Yes, we'll provide detailed cost per token with assumptions about batching, quantization, and prefix cache hit rates. For Dedicated the unit compute cost is lower but you have committed cost. We'll include a runbook showing cost drivers.
[12:02] Samir: On KMS, we use an enterprise HSM — can Redwood integrate with our HSM provider?
[12:12] Maya: We integrate via standard KMS interfaces and can support HSM-backed keys for Private deployments. We'll capture details in the security pack.
[12:24] [12:40] Speaker 3: Is there any prep we should do on our side to speed up the POC?
[12:47] Ethan: Yes — provide an anonymized subset of production traces, the event schema for your bus, desired JSON schema for outputs, and a list of critical flows. That lets us build the benchmark and the regression tests.
[13:02] Alex: We'll anonymize and share by next week.
[13:08] Lina: Also include a list of stakeholders for the final review.
[13:12] Jordan: I'll invite product ops and legal into the follow-up.
[13:18] 
[13:45] Maya: Quick note on telemetry — we expose tracing headers you can propagate; console will show per-route latency and token breakdown. If you use OpenTelemetry we can export spans to your collector.
[13:58] Priya N.: Good.
[14:02] 
[14:20] Ethan: For the benchmark harness we'll send a repo with scripts that can run locally or in Redwood-hosted env. It includes load generators, prompt templates, and evaluation notebooks.
[14:34] Alex: Will the benchmark include function calling flows where the model triggers external API calls?
[14:44] Ethan: Yes, we can simulate tool invocations and measure end-to-end latency including callback orchestration. We'll also measure success/failure rates for downstream tools.
[14:58] 
[15:15] Speaker 1: Any blockers around data residency or region?
[15:23] Maya: No, we can run everything in eu-west-1. For Private deployments we'll work through your VPC peering rules.
[15:30] Samir: Make sure log retention and deletion policy is explicit.
[15:35] Maya: We'll include that.
[15:40] 
[15:58] Lina: Are there any known limitations with very high qps and streaming tool calls?
[16:08] Ethan: At very high qps streaming with tool calls can add overhead; we recommend batching where semantics allow and using async callbacks for heavy tasks. We'll map tradeoffs in the playbook.
[16:22] 
[17:00] Maya: Let's capture the acceptance criteria live: P95 < 350ms for 1k qps baseline with 3x burst acceptable, entity extraction F1 > 0.92, schema compliance > 98%, region eu-west-1, SOC2, KMS, SSO. Anything to add?
[17:22] Jordan: Add cost per 1M tokens target range — we'll review after you send the model assumptions.
[17:30] 
[17:45] Ethan: We'll draft a POC playbook and post it in the shared drive. It will include the benchmark plan, test data, metrics, and sample SDK snippets for Java and Python.
[17:58] Priya Chen: Also include sample rollbacks and fallback policies in the playbook.
[18:05] Maya: Noted.
[18:10] 
[18:40] Alex: Quick tech detail — do you provide SAML SSO and RBAC at route level?
[18:48] Maya: Yes SSO (SAML / OIDC) and RBAC at least at token and route granularity. We'll provide RBAC mappings example.
[18:58] Samir: And can we get per-request PII redaction options?
[19:06] Ethan: We have built-in redaction hooks and can plug in your redaction pipelines. For Private you'll have more control.
[19:20] 
[19:45] Jordan: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[19:50] Maya: Recap: 1) Redwood sends security pack and network diagram (Maya) 2) Redwood sends benchmark harness and templates (Ethan) 3) Catalyst provides anonymized prompt traces and stakeholder list (Alex/Jordan) 4) Schedule benchmark kickoff week of 2026-11-16. Does that match?
[20:12] Jordan: Yes.
[20:14] Priya N.: One more ask — can you include a short runbook for production cutover and canarying?
[20:22] Maya: We'll add a canary plan and canary metric thresholds.
[20:30] 
[20:55] Ethan: Any final questions?
[21:00] Lina: No, thanks this was helpful.
[21:05] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of meeting.
